prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT prescribe aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) — risk of precipitating myasthenic crisis
Do NOT prescribe fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — FDA black-box warning for MG exacerbation
Do NOT prescribe telithromycin — contraindicated in MG
Do NOT administer IV magnesium for MG patients (e.g., for hypomagnesaemia, eclampsia prophylaxis) without alternative — blocks NMJ transmission
Do NOT use non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers without anaesthesia/MG-aware dosing protocols
Do NOT initiate high-dose corticosteroids as sole outpatient therapy without hospitalization or pyridostigmine bridge — risk of paradoxical worsening at days 5-10
Do NOT attribute fluctuating fatigable weakness to a functional disorder before completing serology + RNS + single-fiber EMG workup
Do NOT escalate hydroxychloroquine to high dose during MG initial workup — rare exacerbation reports.

avoided_actions.rationale: MG is a peripheral neuromuscular junction disorder; EEG has no diagnostic role.
No CSF role in MG; LP risks complications without diagnostic yield.
Advanced imaging (PET/MR spectroscopy/perfusion) is not indicated for MG diagnosis or staging; CT chest covers thymoma screening.
Brain MRI is non-contributory in typical MG; reserve for cases where an alternative CNS cause (brainstem lesion, demyelination) is genuinely in the differential.
Echocardiography is not indicated for MG unless a comorbid cardiac question exists.
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated for MG unless arrhythmia or autonomic disease is independently suspected.

accepted: Myasthenia gravis, generalized (MGFA Class IIb), AChR antibody-positive, without thymoma, in setting of SLE/Sjögren overlap (polyautoimmunity)

differential.key_features: SLE can produce myopathy with fatigability; CK was normal (118) and RNS shows decrement consistent with NMJ rather than myopathy.
Sjögren can cause neuropathy but does not produce fatigable ptosis/diplopia or RNS decrement.
LEMS shows low baseline CMAP with >100% facilitation; here baseline CMAP normal, no SCLC history, anti-VGCC negative expected.
Patient not on penicillamine; statins can cause myopathy but not fatigable bulbar weakness.
No focal neurological signs other than fatigable cranial weakness; pattern inconsistent with focal CNS lesion.

key_clinical_evidence: Fluctuating, fatigable weakness with diurnal pattern (worse evening) is the clinical hallmark of MG — fixed weakness suggests an alternative diagnosis.
Ocular involvement (ptosis, diplopia) is asymmetric and fatigable in MG; thyroid eye disease causes restrictive (not fatigable) ophthalmoplegia.
Single-fiber EMG (sensitivity >95%) is the most sensitive electrodiagnostic test — order when RNS is non-diagnostic or serology is negative.
All confirmed MG cases require CT chest for thymoma — present in roughly 10-15% of generalized MG; thymectomy (MGTX trial) improves long-term outcomes in non-thymoma AChR+ MG as well.
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers can precipitate myasthenic crisis and must be screened against any new prescription.
Polyautoimmunity (SLE + Sjögren + MG) is well described — coexistence supports rather than refutes MG diagnosis.
Borderline RNS (8-10%) plus borderline AChR titer (0.6 nmol/L) is a paradigmatic indication for single-fiber EMG.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mild SLE activity does not explain fatigable ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia, or RNS decrement; AChR antibodies are diagnostic; SLE comorbidity is real but separate.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Dismiss as a non-specific positive in the setting of polyautoimmunity.

patient.chief_complaint: Fluctuating ptosis, diplopia, and difficulty swallowing liquids

past_medical_history: Systemic lupus erythematosus (stable, skin and joint involvement only)

patient.history_present_illness: A 48-year-old woman with known SLE and Sjögren syndrome was referred to neurology after her rheumatologist noticed bilateral ptosis during a routine follow-up visit. She reports that she first noticed drooping of her right eyelid approximately 5 months ago, which she attributed to fatigue related to her lupus. She initially thought her Sjögren syndrome dry eyes were causing the eyelid heaviness. The ptosis became bilateral over 3 months and was accompanied by intermittent double vision, worse at the end of the day and on sustained lateral gaze. She mentions she has been having trouble swallowing liquids — she occasionally coughs when drinking water rapidly but can swallow solid foods without major difficulty. Her neck feels weak and she has been supporting her chin with her hand during prolonged reading. She initially discussed these symptoms with her rheumatologist, who increased her hydroxychloroquine dose thinking it was a lupus flare — this did not improve the neurological symptoms. She denies headache, sensory loss, or limb weakness at rest, though she notices she tires easily when blow-drying her hair (arm fatigue with overhead activities). She has not had any infections recently. She has a maternal aunt with myasthenia gravis, which her rheumatologist recalled and prompted the neurology referral. Her lupus has been otherwise stable — no joint flares, no rash worsening, no renal involvement. She is on hydroxychloroquine long-term and has had normal ophthalmology retinal checks.

neurological_exam.additional: No respiratory distress at rest. NIF -38 cmH2O. FVC 78% predicted. Neck weakness notable — patient cannot lift head off pillow against resistance.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral ptosis, right greater than left. Fatigable ptosis on sustained upgaze — ptosis becomes complete on right side at 55 seconds. Diplopia on upgaze and rightward gaze. Mild right eye adduction weakness. Pupils equal and reactive. Mild dysarthria after sustained speech (>2 minutes). No facial sensory deficit. Palate symmetric at rest but slight nasal regurgitation of water on examination.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal casual gait. Mild waddling pattern on prolonged walking.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Normal language and cognition.
neurological_exam.motor: Proximal upper extremity: deltoids 4/5 bilaterally. Neck flexors: 3+/5. Distal strength preserved. Demonstrable fatigability — neck flexion strength drops from 3+ to 3-/5 after 30 seconds sustained effort.
